1:
The discourse is undated and they place it differently. Gill says plainly that when it was, under what reign, and what interval separates it from the preceding chapter are not known, resting only on its being from the Lord. Clarke assigns it to the first year of Zedekiah on the authority of a modern chronologer. Ellicott reasons from internal evidence to a much earlier point, probably the reign of Josiah, on two grounds: the Chaldean invasion is not so near as in the chapter before, and the prophet still lives at Anathoth, as the closing verses show. He records that some critics prefer the reign of Jehoiachin instead. Keil and Delitzsch leave the date alone and map the structure: a first part on disloyalty to the covenant, a second beginning with the plot at Anathoth, a third in the chapter following.

What covenant is meant is a second question. Ellicott holds that the phrase had acquired a definite and special sense from the discovery of the lost book of the Law under Josiah and the covenant the people then entered into. Gill reports that reading and prefers another, taking it for the law of Moses itself, or the covenant at Horeb, or rather the one made in Moab; Wesley likewise makes it the covenant of the law delivered by Moses, to which the people more than once promised obedience. Clarke suggests something more concrete, that the prophet may have had the words of the desert covenant read aloud on this occasion, or at least the blessings and cursings pronounced when the people first entered the land.

That the opening summons is plural interests two of them. Gill takes it as addressed not to Jeremiah alone but to others with him, perhaps the other prophets of his day, or Baruch, or the priests at Anathoth, while allowing that Hebrew often puts one number for another and that one version renders it singular. Calvin reads the plural as evidence that a few assistants remained: though good men were very few, the prophet was not without colleagues who confirmed his doctrine, and though he excelled them there was no emulation, for he willingly admitted into fellowship all whom he found united in so good and holy a cause.

Henry frames the whole as a legal proceeding, the prophet acting as prosecutor in God's name and drawing up an indictment against wilful disobedience. He has him open the charter on which their standing rested, since they had forgotten its tenour and lived as though the grant were absolute, or as though the ceremonial observances were all that was required, when the thing insisted on was obedience, which was better than sacrifice. Calvin makes the same move for another purpose: setting their departure from the law before them was to assure them their quarrel was not with Jeremiah but with Moses and with God; and he applies it to disputants of his own day who repudiate what is adduced from law and prophets while professing to receive whatever proceeds from God.

The curse itself is where Ellicott is most exact. He calls the verse a mosaic of phrases taken with slight verbal changes from the recently discovered book of the Law, and observes that the curse is practically identical with one there except that a word meaning obeys has replaced one meaning confirms. On the iron furnace he notes that the word denotes a smelter's furnace and stands for Egypt, but that the brick-kiln furnaces in which the people had actually laboured probably gave the phrase its special force. Clarke supposes that after the reading the prophet summed the matter up, and puts the summary in a sentence: the man is cursed who does not obey and blessed who does, and from these declarations God will not depart.
4:
The land promised to the fathers is not, for Calvin, the substance of the promise. Canaan is mentioned only as the pledge of God's favour, since the words that he would be their God and they his people already include eternal life and celestial glory, and to fasten on the territory alone would be a frigid view. Ellicott approaches the same phrase historically. The description of a land flowing with milk and honey appears first in the exodus narrative and quickly became proverbial, and he notices what the terms imply: the plenty of a pastoral rather than an agricultural people, belonging to the earlier stages of Israel's life rather than the later. Gill identifies the fathers to whom the oath was sworn as the three patriarchs.

The prophet's answering word is read three ways. Ellicott makes it liturgical, the Amen of Israel's litanies, brought into fresh prominence by the newly found book and uttered by princes and people at the solemn ceremony under Josiah. Clarke turns it into a double petition, that the promises be fulfilled and that the incorrigible beware of the threatenings. Wesley leaves the choice open: God having ended his speech, the prophet says Amen either as asserting the truth of what had been said or as wishing that the people would act according to their covenant. Keil and Delitzsch treat the same stretch structurally, heading what follows as the people's breach of the covenant and its consequences.

The command to proclaim the words in the cities is taken literally by two of them. Ellicott thinks the prophet actually went from city to city as a preacher of repentance, taking the newly discovered book for his text, and points out that a royal progress through the kingdom to destroy the high places is recorded for the same period, which such a discourse would fitly accompany. Clarke supposes the covenant with its blessings and cursings read in every city and street so that all might know their duty, their privileges and their danger. Calvin instead imagines the reception: the people object that they are the disciples of Moses, taught the law from childhood, and tell the prophet to take himself off to the Chaldeans or the Egyptians, since they understand what the law teaches.

His answer is that so great an oblivion had prevailed that they no longer knew what God had taught, and that they and their fathers alike needed teaching over again, like children kept at the rudiments and never making progress. On the protesting that follows Calvin finds a legal figure, God submitting himself as it were to a third party's judgment, as men protest before a tribunal, and doing so not once but across every generation from the exodus onward. The rising early he refuses to take transitively, as some do, and explains it as God applying to himself what properly belonged to his prophets. Ellicott adds that the phrase in this spiritual sense is almost peculiar to this prophet, who uses it twelve times.

Two words in the last verse are contested. Ellicott gives the first its harder sense, stubbornness rather than imagination, and changes the tense of the threat: it should read that God has brought these things upon them, so the clause is not a direct prediction but an appeal to past experience as foreshadowing what is to come. Wesley keeps the future and the threat, taking it that God will bring upon them all the words of threatening annexed to the covenant. Calvin fixes on their refusal to incline the ear: a man may hear another and not do what he says, yet still show some courtesy, but to close every avenue and forbid another to speak at all is an intolerable barbarity. Gill notes that the warnings had been repeated again and again, which aggravates the stubbornness.
9:
Whether the conspiracy is a real one divides them. Ellicott takes it as literal and political: the words explain the rapid apostasy that followed Josiah's death, and show that all through the reforming years there had been an organised though secret resistance to the policy the king represented. Clarke reads it much the same, as men become sworn brothers, determined to cast off the divine yoke and no longer have God reign over them. Wesley reduces it to a figure, that all sorts of people acted alike, as if they had conspired together to break the law. Calvin keeps it real but presses the verb: the thing has been discovered, as thieves are caught in the very act, so it is no longer disputable whether the people had deliberately perverted the worship of God.

Calvin then makes the charge comparative. When the people first fell together into ungodly superstitions there was more excuse for it, since they had not yet struck deep roots in true religion; but after God had tried many times to bring them back, and all that diligence proved fruitless, what remained was a confirmed and hopeless obstinacy. Gill and Clarke supply the recent history that makes the point concrete. Both recall the reformation under Josiah, when the idols were abolished and the high places mostly destroyed, and both observe that under his successors the people returned to the idolatries of earlier reigns. Clarke adds the bleakest sentence here, that it required a captivity to cure the propensity, that God sent one, and that after it there was no idolatry among the Jews.

The word rendered forefathers is examined by two of them and given the same sense. Ellicott says the Hebrew is more specific and means their first fathers, referring particularly to the idolatries of the wilderness years and the first settlement; he adds that the pronoun in the next clause is emphatically repeated, pointing back to the men of the prophet's own day. Calvin rejects the rendering ancestors as not expressing the point, argues that the word means first rather than former, and offers two constructions, one making it the fathers with whom the covenant was made at the exodus, the other taking it in apposition so that the phrase names the first men who refused to hear.

On the evil that is coming they agree it cannot be got out of. Keil and Delitzsch sharpen the promise: it is not merely that they will fail to escape safely, but that within the calamity they will find no way of rescue at all. Henry draws the rule, that those who will not submit to God's government cannot escape his wrath, there being no fleeing from his justice; and he notes the bitter turn by which men in affliction seek the God they had slighted. Gill observes that the evil threatened is punishment for the evil of sin, and that no evil of that kind is other than of God's sending. Clarke refers the crying to the gods back to an earlier chapter.

Calvin finds a difficulty in the sequence and answers it twice. First, how can they cry to God and to foreign gods at once? Because the unbelieving mind in a turbulent state turns here and there and lays hold of nothing fixed; and he thinks the plainest reading is that they cry to God first and, unheard, turn to the others. Second, if they all worshipped one idol, where is the multitude of gods the verse condemns? His answer is that the name is a common one, meaning a patron or inferior god who procures the supreme God's favour, so every idol bore it. Wesley gives the same etymology, from a word for lord, and notes its use across several nations. Ellicott identifies the shameful thing as the image set up openly in every city and street.
14:
The prohibition on praying is read as evidence of what the prophet had been doing. Calvin infers it directly: had he not been diligent in prayer it would not have been necessary to forbid him, so the verse shows him in a twofold character, thundering against the despisers as herald of vengeance while supplicating pardon for lost men. Ellicott adds the reason for refusal in a phrase: it is at once too early and too late for that prayer, since the people have not yet been moved to repentance and their cry is simply the wail of suffering, so the discipline must do its work. Gill argues the words are less a prohibition of the prophet than a threatening to the people, who lose the benefit even of good men's prayers. Clarke says only that their measure is full.

The next verse is the hardest in the chapter, beginning with a term of endearment nobody can place with confidence. Gill reports it taken as the prophet's own words, meaning that God, his beloved, has no business remaining in a sanctuary the people have defiled, and mentions a reading making it Christ withdrawing from the temple; his alternative is that God speaks of the Jews, beloved for their fathers' sake. Clarke reports a tradition referring it to Abraham or Moses, whose intercession was powerful, the point being that even they would not now be regarded, and an alternative making it an endearment belonging to Israel as espoused to God. Wesley takes that last without hesitation, with God speaking as the husband he formerly was.

Calvin is unusually forthright here. He grants that the words are concise and that brevity is commonly obscure, which is why interpreters have gone various ways; but he holds that the almost universally received explanation, making the prophet the speaker and the temple his house, is wrong, that the Targum applies the words to God far more correctly, and that anyone considering them wisely will wonder so many learned men were mistaken on a point by no means doubtful. He adds that the endearment is ironical, given how unworthy the people were. Ellicott, on the same clause, judges the Hebrew difficult and probably corrupt, offers a rendering and a conjectural emendation, and observes that the word translated lewdness means primarily a plan, then a scheme in a bad sense.

Whatever the details, Ellicott thinks the general sense clear, that a religion of mere ritual and sacrifices will not avail to save. Wesley reaches it from the other end, that flesh set before idols as well as before God became polluted, and notes the sting in the closing clause, that they were not only evil but gloried in it. On the olive that follows there is agreement about what the figure grants before it takes away. Keil and Delitzsch call Judah a noble planting of God's, take the fruit for the nation in its individual members, and observe that the reversal comes without any adversative particle, which makes it the more abrupt and violent.

Ellicott reads the naming of the name as the divine purpose in the calling and election of Israel, what she was meant to be and made no effort to become. Clarke puts it plainly, that God made them like a green olive and they degenerated. Gill allows that the tree bore the fruit of good works for a time. Calvin turns the last verse into a question: is your beauty from yourselves, or has all your dignity proceeded from God's gratuitous kindness, so that he who planted the tree may pull it up when he pleases? He derides the confidence that answered such warnings by appealing to the temple as God's own resting place for ever. Ellicott lays the same stress on the planter, who bestowed every condition of fruitfulness and now passes the sentence himself.
18:
How the prophet learned of the plot is where Henry is best. None of his friends could tell him and none of his enemies would, so he came to Anathoth meaning no harm and fearing none, with but a step between him and death; God showed him their doings, and such were the devices that discovering them was defeating them. He adds why the warning mattered beyond the man: had God let him walk into it, his enemies would have urged that one who foretold his country's ruin could not foresee his own peril. Clarke says the same briefly, that God gave a secret warning to put him on his guard. Ellicott finds the section opening abruptly and infers the plots had only just come to his notice.

Why his townsmen turned on him is answered two ways. Ellicott traces a sequence: they first tried threats, as an earlier prophet had been ordered out of a royal sanctuary, and only when that failed conspired against his life. Calvin gives the motive rather than the sequence, that men who dare not blaspheme God assail his servants instead and pretend the quarrel is with them; and he hears the same clamour in his own day, when reproof of hidden vices is met by demanding to know who told the preacher, and whether he has an oracle from heaven. Henry notes the aggravation that Anathoth was a priest's city and malignant nonetheless, and that the plot, though cruel, was baffled: the prophet outlived most of his enemies and his memory outlived them all.

The comparison he makes for himself turns on one word, and all who touch it correct the English. Gill observes that the disjunctive is absent from the Hebrew, so the second noun is better taken as an adjective, and lists versions offering tame, harmless and clean. Ellicott agrees the translators mistook an adjective for a noun, and renders it a tame lamb reared in its master's house; assuming the earlier date of that passage, he hears an allusion to the sufferer described there. Clarke presses the word furthest, deriving from a cognate the sense of a creature accustomed, familiar, a companion and intimate friend, then turns it on the story: the men of Anathoth were his townsmen, he was bred among them, they were his familiar friends, and now they lay wait for his life.

What they meant to destroy was more than the man. Ellicott notes that the Hebrew says the tree with its bread, taken for fruit, though some render it sap, and judges the phrase proverbial for total destruction, of the man and of his work. Henry expands it the same way, an intent to destroy root and branch, both the prophet and the prophecy, killing the one and defeating the other. Clarke puts it in a sentence: they meant to slay the prophet so his prophecies would end. Wesley observes that the conspiracy is mentioned nowhere else, and that the aim was to end not the prophesying only but the life.

The imprecation that follows is handled with unusual care. Clarke removes the difficulty by changing the mood: not let me see, but I shall see the punishment inflicted. Ellicott declines that escape and judges the prayer directly: it belongs to an earlier stage of the religious life, before indignation is tempered by the law of forgiveness, and so is not to be imitated, but neither hastily condemned, since appealing to a higher judge is itself a victory over the impulse to take vengeance oneself. Henry reports both verdicts without settling between them. Calvin resolves the inconsistency by distinguishing private feeling from zeal: the prophet disregarded his own life and was unmoved by private wrongs, but was nevertheless not a log of wood. Keil and Delitzsch note that the searcher of hearts therefore knows he has done no evil.
